ef65c69e286641c0.en_html: There is a moment I will never forget. On the final day of IDFC2014, we held a workshop for students at the University of Yangon to share with the wider public what we had learned and achieved during one week of activities. That year’s topic was “Career Development,” so IDFC participants and local university students worked together to share our ideas on how to become a good leader through games and physical activities. One girl who took part was deeply moved by our workshop and said, “I want to do activities like this too!” Inspired by the workshop, she volunteered to join the Myanmar-side executive committee for 2016 and went on to handle public relations, just as I did, in the following year’s activities. I was truly surprised. That was the first time I realized that my activities had moved someone. It may have been a small thing in terms of society as a whole, but I believe it had an impact that changed her life. A workshop created by a student like me had moved someone—that moment really gave me goosebumps.

2889e59ac0e7724e.en_html: I first learned about IDFC through a friend from my undergraduate years. She had participated in IDFC2014 and told me, “It was really great!” At first, I did not pay it much attention, but she brought it up again before recruitment for IDFC2016 began. When I looked into it, I found that the theme that year was “Community Development,” and it immediately struck a chord. I am studying development studies at a graduate school in Switzerland, but most graduate study happens at a desk. That alone cannot show you the realities of developing countries, and I wanted to use all five senses to find out whether what I had read in the literature was true. The IDFC theme happened to match what I had been hoping for, and I got excited all by myself in my apartment in Geneva, thinking, “I have to participate!” (laughs)

ba49c3ee330ec9b1.en_html: Aki: “I began studying development studies after entering university, with particular opportunities to learn through studying abroad and seminars. My interest began in high school, when my English teacher told us about the civil wars in Cambodia and Rwanda and about the United Nations. The university in London where I later chose to study abroad was also well known in international development studies. Through my studies there, I began wanting to work in the field myself. The region I initially wanted to see firsthand was Southeast Asia. With those thoughts in mind, I returned to Japan, and around May, after finishing my job search, I was asked whether I would like to help run IDFC. I decided without hesitation to become an organizer.”

27feecde656d7ef2.en_html: I had various worries at first too. Of course, I had never been to Myanmar, and I had never visited a developing country for anything other than travel. I wondered, “Will I be able to manage…?” While all the other participants were joining from Japan, I also wondered what people would think of me being the only one joining from Geneva, where I was studying abroad. But once I actually participated, all those worries turned out to be unfounded. I want to convey that if you take that step with a purpose, all sorts of things await you at IDFC, and you can discover things you have never seen before.

1c20e8d1236a6ff2.en_html: There are also many fascinating people at IDFC. Talking with other participants about our past experiences and our futures may have had an even greater impact on me than the individual projects. I met many friends whom I can continue to see even after the program ends, encouraging each other toward our respective goals. I also came to feel that I should work hard so that I can be active on the same stage as these people. If there is something you want to achieve, why not seize the opportunity IDFC offers and embark on a new adventure? You are sure to discover something important.
